Listen · Module 7 overview
Decoding the Critic: The Myth of Neutrality
Module 7 · Block 2: Reviewing Theatre

Who reviews, and for whom?

How cultural context shapes criticism — and what that reveals about every reviewer in the room

"There are so many Australians — including kids and teenagers — who still don't see stories resembling theirs on screen, who see very few people who look like their families. To not feel visible or reflected is a quietly dehumanising process. And though we might congratulate ourselves on doing better at diversity, Australia is far behind."
— Benjamin Law, writer (in Diversity Arts Australia, Shifting the Balance, 2019)
What this module asks you to do

Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

01
Understand that no reviewer is neutral — everyone brings assumptions shaped by their background, and those assumptions affect what they see on stage.
02
Explain who holds power in Australian arts criticism and why that matters, using evidence from national research.
03
Sit inside a genuine disagreement about reviewing practice and hold both sides of the argument at once.
04
Tell the difference between a production that isn't working and a production you don't have the framework to read yet.
05
Name your own position as a reviewer — what you bring into the theatre, and how that shapes your response to what you see.
Section 1

Where Module 6 stopped, and why we have to keep going

Module 6 treated reviewing as a practice that can be studied and improved. It looked at how to watch closely, how to hold your own taste at arm's length long enough to evaluate what the work is actually doing, how to put something as fugitive as a live performance into words another person can follow. None of that goes away in this module. What Module 7 does is notice the thing Module 6 leaves out.

Every reviewer who walks into a theatre brings more than a notebook. They bring a sense of what good theatre sounds like, an inherited map of whose stories count as serious and whose get treated as supplementary, and a set of trained instincts for what "excellence" looks like on a stage. Some of this comes from cultural background. Some from formal education. Some is simply the accumulated weight of traditions and canons a reviewer has grown up inside without ever having chosen them.

Module 6 asked how you review. Module 7 asks a harder question. Who is doing the reviewing in the first place, whose perspective has been treated as the authoritative one, and what happens when the work on stage comes from a cultural world the reviewer does not share?

Section 2

What the national data actually shows

Arguments about diversity in arts criticism drift quickly into anecdote and impression, so it is worth starting with something harder. In 2019, Diversity Arts Australia published Shifting the Balance, the first national study to measure cultural diversity in the leadership of Australia's major arts, screen and creative organisations. The researchers examined 1,980 people holding leadership positions across 200 of the country's most influential cultural institutions.

9%
Cultural leadership, nationally
39% of the population, 9% of the leaders

Around thirty-nine per cent of Australians come from a culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) background. Only nine per cent of the leaders across those 200 institutions do. Non-CALD Australians are nine times more likely to hold a position of cultural leadership than their share of the population would predict. Close to half of the organisations studied had zero CALD representation whatsoever at the leadership level. Not one board member. Not one executive. Not one creative director.

5%
Performing arts: worst of all
The bottom of an already dismal picture

Across every sector the study examined, performing arts came in worst. Only five per cent of performing arts leaders came from a CALD background, against a national figure of thirty-nine per cent. Close to two thirds of performing arts organisations had no CALD leaders at all. If you happen to be a culturally diverse Australian, you are eight times less likely to hold a leadership role in this sector than your share of the population would suggest.

80%
The participation paradox
More engaged, less represented

CALD Australians are not absent from the arts. They are, on average, more engaged with them than the general population. The Australia Council's national participation survey found that eighty per cent of Australians from culturally diverse backgrounds participate in the arts, compared with seventy-two per cent of the mainstream population. The audiences are diverse. The decision-makers are not.

Between the audience and the stage sits the critic, whose presence on opening night is part of what determines which shows get sustained attention, which artists are taken seriously, and which aesthetic assumptions come to be treated as the default standard. When that critical corps is drawn almost entirely from one cultural background, the conversation itself gets shaped — in its assumptions and its reference points — by a narrow band speaking in effect on behalf of everyone.

Source: Diversity Arts Australia, BYP Group and Western Sydney University. 2019. Shifting the Balance. Sydney.

Before you read about what happened in Melbourne in 2023, take a moment. If you were an arts editor and a creative team asked you to assign only a reviewer who shared their cultural background — what would you do? Hold that answer. You'll need it.

Section 3

seven methods of killing kylie jenner and the Melbourne reviewing controversy of 2023

In January 2023, Jasmine Lee-Jones's award-winning play opened at Malthouse Theatre in Melbourne. It follows two Black women in the UK as they get caught up in a social media firestorm after one of them publicly contests Kylie Jenner's claim to the status of "self-made billionaire." It is fierce and very funny, and uncompromising in what it takes on: colourism, queerness, cultural appropriation, and the commodification of Black womanhood.

Iolanthe and Chika Ikogwe in seven methods of killing kylie jenner at Malthouse Theatre. Image: Malthouse Theatre.

A second storm was building outside the theatre. The creative team — co-directors Zindzi Okenyo (Kenyan Australian) and Shari Sebbens (Bardi and Jabirr Jabirr woman), alongside actor and community engagement consultant Moreblessing Maturure (Zimbabwean Australian) — made a public request: that the show be reviewed only by critics of colour.

Sebbens, speaking to SBS News, framed the request plainly. "It's never been about a positive bias. It's never been about expecting a person of colour to respond well to the piece. It's actually just been about getting a critic of colour a job." Okenyo added that the team wanted "to make sure Black, Indigenous, and people of colour have the opportunity to review a show that aligned with their own lived experience." The request was less about matching identity to material than about using a particular production to crack open a reviewing economy that has rarely hired outside one pool.

The Age declined to review the production. The paper's arts editor, Elizabeth Flux, herself Hong Kong-born and Eurasian, explained the decision in an opinion piece. Her argument was that the right response to a lack of diversity in criticism is to have "more voices speaking up on everything," not to match the identity of the reviewer to the identity of the work. She worried that the request was tokenistic, and that it risked treating people of colour as a monolith with one shared experience. "Good critics," she wrote, "irrespective of their lived experience, put their biases to one side and identify what does and doesn't work in a piece of art."

There is no clean resolution to this dispute. Flux is right that a healthy critical culture needs more voices across everything, and that matching critics to productions by identity would be a thin version of diversity. The creative team is right that the field is structurally unequal, that new voices sometimes require deliberate structural support if they are to enter at all, and that "neutrality" is a great deal easier to assert when it happens to coincide with what the room already assumes.

Sebbens replied directly: "It is impossible to leave your biases at the door. If we could do that, we wouldn't have deaths in custody, we wouldn't have the discrepancies we have in health, in education, in literacy the world over for Black and brown and Indigenous people. Acknowledge it, put it in your review, talk about what it means for you."

The case matters because it forces a question that sits directly beneath your own assessments: when you walk into the theatre to see the productions in this subject, what are you actually walking in with, and how does that shape what you notice, what you value, and what you miss entirely?

Section 4

First Nations performance and the question of who has the authority to evaluate it

Nowhere in Australia is the question of who gets to tell, interpret and evaluate stories more charged than in relation to First Nations performance. This is not a diversity question in the reducible sense. It sits inside a larger set of questions about sovereignty, cultural authority, and a history of dispossession that reaches directly into how stories are made, owned, and received on Australian stages.

Rachael Maza on ownership: the law protects the writer, not the Auntie

In a TEDx talk at Castlemaine, Rachael Maza — a Yidinji, Meriam and Dutch woman, and for seventeen years Artistic Director of ILBIJERRI Theatre Company in Melbourne — laid out a deceptively simple set of questions. Whose story is it? Who owns it? Who has the authority to tell it? And who gets the credit — along with the royalties?

Her example takes the abstraction and sharpens it. An Auntie tells her story to a non-Indigenous writer, who then shapes it into a book through research, editing and craft. Under Australian copyright law, the writer owns that story entirely: the copyright, the royalties, the awards, and what Maza calls the reputation of being "an expert in the subject of Auntie." If the Auntie disagrees with how she has been represented — if the book is culturally inaccurate or even culturally unsafe — she has no legal recourse. She has no copyright. She is, as Maza puts it, completely powerless.

Watch · 11 minutes
Rachael Maza, 'Who Owns the Story?', TEDxCastlemaine, 2024. As you watch, pay attention to the numbats — and to the moment Maza names what went wrong.

Maza turns to the Australian Opera's adaptation of The Rabbits, Shaun Tan and John Marsden's picture book that tells the story of colonisation from the perspective of the colonised — the numbats. In the book, the numbats narrate their own experience. In the opera, the narration was handed to a character not in the original book at all: a fluffy white bird, chosen because that character had the good singing voice. It looks like ordinary theatrical licence. What it did, Maza argues, was take voice and agency away from the colonised — precisely the structural choice the book had been built around.

"They were all good people, all really talented, amazing people, and I'm pretty sure no one intended any ill intentions. And it was such an easy mistake to make. But the implications for us as black fellas was massive. They basically just weren't aware of their subconscious bias."
— Rachael Maza, 'Who owns the story?', TEDxCastlemaine, 2024

The dynamic she names sits directly under the work of criticism. A reviewer who evaluates First Nations work without a working sense of its cultural logic — without knowing whose story it is, what protocols attend it, or what dramaturgical decisions are carrying cultural weight — can end up doing precisely what the opera's team did: making a choice that looks defensible from inside one framework while stripping the work of the thing it was trying to do.

Carissa Lee on the failure mode that does the most damage

Carissa Lee, a First Nations emerging critic writing for the Witness Performance platform, makes the same argument from the reviewer's chair. She traces how Indigenous performance in Australia has been framed by non-Indigenous critics since the nineteenth century: first as anthropological curiosity, then as something to be measured against European theatrical convention, and only rarely on its own terms. The failure mode she names is specific, and it is the one that does the most quiet damage. It is the confusion of unfamiliarity with artistic failure.

Lee's example cuts straight through. When Cameron Woodhead reviewed Shadow King, an Indigenous retelling of Shakespeare's King Lear, he criticised the adaptation for not staying close enough to Shakespeare's language and dramatic structure. Lee's response: "How, while discussing a harrowing story of greed, violence, and betrayal leading to the eventual annihilation of a man's family, can a reviewer not just take a sec to shed his need for the familiar Shakespearean experience?" Other reviewers, including the Indigenous writer Celeste Liddle, noticed what Woodhead missed altogether — most notably the way the army presence in the production was pulling the Northern Territory Intervention into the frame of the play.

Lee is not suggesting that non-Indigenous writers stop reviewing Indigenous work. She is insisting they prepare properly. "Although whitefellas may not necessarily know the nuances and cultural loads of shows put together by people of colour, it's nevertheless important that they write about them." What she requires is symmetry of effort. "When I get to review a white show, you can bet I'll be up late finding out everything I can about the creators, their processes, and why they long to create the stories they do."

"Critics need to be able to identify cultural differences in a production, and to be able to make the distinction between what is unsuccessful in its delivery and what is unfamiliar. One is often confused for the other."
— Carissa Lee, 'The importance of informed reviewers', Witness Performance, 2018

Cultural authority, protocols, and what responsible engagement actually asks

Behind Maza's and Lee's arguments sits a broader framework of cultural obligation. The Australia Council's Protocols for Using First Nations Cultural and Intellectual Property in the Arts (third edition, 2019), developed by Dr Terri Janke, offers practical guidance for anyone working with Indigenous cultural material — including those writing about it in public. The protocols establish that Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property extends well beyond tangible objects to encompass stories, ceremonies, performances, and the knowledge systems that hold them together. This is not raw material available for any passer-by to interpret. Engaging with it responsibly means knowing who the custodians are, what obligations attach to the material, and what the work is attempting on its own terms.

For breadth students meeting these ideas for the first time, the takeaway runs something like this. When you are watching a First Nations production — or reading a review of one — the useful question is not just "was it good?" It is "good by whose standards, evaluated within which framework, and with what understanding of what this work is actually trying to do?" That is not a lower bar. It is, demonstrably, a higher one.

Section 5

Does cultural literacy lower the standard of criticism, or raise it?

There is a lazy version of the positionality argument that ends somewhere unhelpful. If every reviewer is shaped by their cultural background, then no one can fairly evaluate work from outside their own, and criticism either becomes impossible or collapses into a performance of politeness. If that were really the conclusion, we should all go home.

It is not the conclusion any of the critics and scholars in this module are drawing. What they are arguing is something more demanding: cultural literacy raises the standard of criticism rather than lowering it. You cannot seriously evaluate what you do not understand, and the work of understanding is itself a form of critical rigour.

Alison Croggon and the "cookie cutter" problem

In her 2014 essay 'The Critical Gap,' the Melbourne critic Alison Croggon identifies what she calls a "cookie cutter attitude to reviewing theatre" — the assumption that one evaluative template applies to every production. Productions which operate otherwise — whose storytelling moves differently or whose relationship to an audience is organised around a different set of cultural expectations — end up being measured against standards they were never trying to meet, and duly found wanting.

Croggon argues that the consumer-driven reduction of criticism to thumbs-up or thumbs-down amounts to a form of censorship — not active silencing, but a structural inability to say anything complex about work that does not fit the expected mould.

What rigorous, culturally literate criticism looks like in practice

Chido Mwat, a Zimbabwean Australian writer and performer, reviewed seven methods of killing kylie jenner for ArtsHub. Mwat does not treat the production gently because it was made by artists of colour. She evaluates the directing decisions, the use of projection and physical comedy, the technical design, and the dramaturgical structure with the kind of attention any reviewer would be expected to bring. She is also, unmistakably, reading from a position of cultural literacy. She recognises the Afrobeats and Amapiano playing in the foyer as a deliberate curatorial decision rather than ambient noise. She grasps that the colourism conversation between the two central characters is structurally load-bearing, not incidental to the plot.

Mwat's review is rigorous and culturally informed at the same time. She does not trade one for the other. The choice between evaluative seriousness and cultural literacy is a false binary. The best criticism holds both. The worst — the kind that mistakes its own unfamiliarity for the work's failure — offers neither.

Section 6

The argument beyond race: queer dramaturgies, StoryCasters, and structural change

The question of who reviews and how does not stop at race or cultural background. These sections extend the argument into two further territories.

Queer dramaturgies and the limits of the template
Campbell & Farrier on what happens when the form itself is queer

In their introduction to Queer Dramaturgies, Alyson Campbell (University of Melbourne) and Stephen Farrier argue that queer performance often operates through forms that resist the conventions of mainstream theatre criticism altogether: cabaret, live art, drag, site-specific work. Work that is non-linear, embodied, improvised, or built around the labouring body rather than a scripted character cannot be adequately assessed by a reviewer who reaches for the standard template of plot, character and production values.

Campbell and Farrier argue that what makes a dramaturgy "queer" is not simply that it depicts queer stories but that it challenges the dominant modes of theatrical representation itself. It unsettles the reviewer's assumption that they already know what theatre is supposed to look like. The argument connects directly to Croggon's cookie-cutter problem and to Lee's case about First Nations performance: in each instance, the inherited framework of criticism becomes invisible to the people using it, functioning as a universal standard when it is in fact culturally and historically specific.

StoryCasters and the structural reproduction of exclusion
Building pathways versus reproducing the old ones

Diversity Arts Australia's StoryCasters programme provides training and mentorship for emerging citizen journalists and digital producers from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, with arts reviewing among its strands. The programme has built a community of practice for over sixty-five young producers in Western Sydney and has profiled more than a hundred culturally diverse artists across New South Wales.

Shirley Le, a StoryCasters mentor writing in Overland, tracks the structural barriers these emerging critics continue to meet — including a 2020 episode in which the Sydney Morning Herald allocated the entire $150,000 grant for emerging culture critics to five white writers despite applications from writers of colour. Le's argument is not that the chosen critics were undeserving. It is that the selection structure itself reproduces the exclusion it claims to be addressing.

Section 7

What all of this actually asks of you

None of this requires you to become an expert in First Nations performance, queer dramaturgies, or the politics of Australian arts criticism in order to do well in this subject. What it does ask is something more modest, and more useful, for your assessments and for how you engage with theatre beyond this semester.

When you sit down to write about the MTC productions you attend this semester, you are not writing from nowhere. You are writing from a particular place — shaped by your cultural background, by your prior experience of live theatre or the lack of it, by your assumptions about what a play is supposed to do, and by whatever frameworks this subject has put into your hands along the way. The strongest critical responses are the ones that name this rather than pretend to a neutrality they cannot actually hold. You are not expected to arrive with all the answers. You are expected to know where you are standing.

And when something in a production puzzles you — a dramaturgical decision that does not fit your expectations, or a story told in a way you have not encountered before, or a theatrical convention you do not recognise — the question to ask yourself is not "is this wrong?" The question is "is this unfamiliar, and what would I need to know to understand what it is doing?"

Module 6 gave you the tools for reviewing. Module 7 asks you to notice the hand that holds them.
